# Illustration — Library Analysis

A thin wrapper holding exactly one SVG, passing Move theme tokens into it so a
drawing is themeable, accessible and correctly sized. Promotion candidate from
`packages/docs/src/components/Illustration.tsx`.

Prior art is thin on purpose: nobody else has this component because nobody else
has `check:purity`. In a library where a page may contain raw `<svg>`, no seam is
needed. In Move, inline `<svg>` is a violation with no sanctioned alternative for
a one-off diagram, so the wrapper is the door in the wall.

### Quick Comparison

| | MUI `SvgIcon` | Chakra `Icon` | React Spectrum `IllustratedMessage` |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Props** | `viewBox`, `inheritViewBox`, `color`, `fontSize`, `titleAccess`, `component`, `htmlColor` | `asChild`, plus style props (`boxSize`, `color`) | layout/spacing props only |
| **Compound** | monolithic | monolithic | compound — SVG + `Heading` + `Content` as children |
| **Sizing** | `fontSize` (`small`/`medium`/`large`) — sized in **em**, so it follows type | `boxSize` style prop | none; the illustration sizes itself |
| **Theming** | `currentColor` by default; `color` maps to palette | `currentColor`; `color` takes a token | none exposed — the icon package owns its styling |
| **A11y** | decorative → `aria-hidden`; semantic → `titleAccess` injects `role="img"` + `<title>` | none documented | **caller's job**: `aria-hidden` + `role="presentation"` when a Heading is present, `aria-label`/`role="img"` when alone |
| **Standout** | `titleAccess` — one prop flips decorative ↔ semantic and writes the markup for you | `asChild` — no wrapper element at all | names the decorative case explicitly, which the icon libraries never do |

### Props Detail

#### MUI — `SvgIcon`

| Prop | Type | Default |
|------|------|---------|
| `viewBox` | `string` | `'0 0 24 24'` |
| `inheritViewBox` | `boolean` | `false` |
| `color` | `'inherit' \| 'primary' \| 'secondary' \| 'action' \| 'disabled' \| 'error' \| 'success'` | `'inherit'` |
| `fontSize` | `'inherit' \| 'small' \| 'medium' \| 'large'` | `'medium'` |
| `titleAccess` | `string` | — |
| `htmlColor` | `string` | — |
| `component` | `elementType` | `'svg'` |

```tsx
<SvgIcon color="primary" fontSize="large" titleAccess="Upload">
  <path d="M10 20v-6h4v6h5v-8h3L12 3 2 12h3v8z" />
</SvgIcon>
```

The instructive part is `fontSize`. Sizes are **em-relative**, so an icon tracks
the text it sits beside rather than carrying a pixel size. Wrong for an
illustration — a diagram is not a glyph — but right about the principle: the size
comes from context, not from a number at the call site.

#### Chakra UI — `Icon`

| Prop | Type | Default |
|------|------|---------|
| `asChild` | `boolean` | `false` |
| style props (`boxSize`, `color`, …) | tokens | — |

```tsx
<Icon asChild color="blue.500">
  <MyGlyph />
</Icon>
```

Chakra ships no icons and hands sizing to the style-prop system. Not a model for
Move, which has no style props by design.

#### Adobe React Spectrum — `IllustratedMessage`

| Prop | Type | Default |
|------|------|---------|
| layout/spacing props | — | — |

```tsx
<IllustratedMessage>
  <NotFound />
  <Heading>No results</Heading>
  <Content>Try another search</Content>
</IllustratedMessage>
```

The only library here that treats an illustration as its own thing, and the only
one that states the decorative rule out loud: when a heading is present the SVG
takes `aria-hidden` + `role="presentation"`, because the heading already names
the block and a second name is noise. Move's wrapper should encode that rather
than leaving it to a docs paragraph nobody reads.

### Accessible-name patterns (Deque testing)

- `role="img"` + a child `<title>` referenced by `aria-labelledby` is the most
  reliable pattern across NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver and TalkBack.
- `aria-label` works equally well and buys nothing — more attributes, same result.
- `<desc>` support is **inconsistent**, and it is a *description*, not a name.
- `focusable="false"` was an IE11 workaround and is no longer needed.

**Finding against the prototype.** It puts both ids into `aria-labelledby`:

```tsx
aria-labelledby={descId ? `${titleId} ${descId}` : titleId}
```

That concatenates the description INTO the accessible name, so a screen reader
reads one long run-on name and there is no description left. `<desc>` belongs on
`aria-describedby`. One-line fix, worth catching before it ships as public API.

### The sizing problem

This is the part that is genuinely hard, and where the prototype should change.

**What makes SVG sizing awkward:**

1. An SVG with a `viewBox` and no `width`/`height` has an *aspect ratio* but **no
   intrinsic size** — it sizes to its container.
2. An SVG with **no** `viewBox` has neither, and CSS replaced-element defaults
   take over: 300×150. This is the classic collapse. The prototype already
   requires `viewBox`, which is the single most important decision here — keep it
   required.
3. `height: auto` then works, because the aspect ratio comes from the viewBox.
4. Without an explicit `aspect-ratio`, the box has no height until the SVG is
   parsed — a layout shift on every illustration.
5. Inline SVGs sit on the text baseline and collect a descender gap;
   `display: block` removes it.
6. A scaled SVG scales its `<text>` and its stroke widths with it. A diagram
   rendered at half size has half-size labels, which fall below the body copy
   they sit next to. `vector-effect="non-scaling-stroke"` fixes hairlines;
   nothing fixes the text except not scaling much.

**Where the prototype lands:** `width: 100%` + `max-width` from a `width` variant
(`normal` 36rem / `wide` 48rem / `full` none), plus a `maxWidth` escape hatch.

**Why that is the wrong shape for Move.** Move's layout rule is that a call site
expresses constraints and participation, never a size, and a preference is only
legal if the container can overrule it. `width="wide"` is a size, chosen at the
call site, in a vocabulary that means nothing to the drawing — and two of the
three names ("normal", "wide") are relative to a page width the component cannot
see.

**Recommendation: derive the cap from the drawing; borrow the overrides.**

The `viewBox` already carries the two numbers needed:

```
viewBox="0 0 640 360"
  → aspect-ratio: 640 / 360     (no layout shift, height needs no declaration)
  → max-inline-size: 640px      (never render larger than it was drawn)
  → inline-size: 100%           (shrink freely below that)
```

This satisfies the layout rule exactly: the container can always make it smaller,
and the illustration never imposes a width upward beyond its natural size. It
needs no prop, invents no vocabulary, and cannot drift from the artwork because
it IS the artwork's numbers. An illustration that should render bigger than it
was drawn is one that should be drawn bigger.

**But "the container constrains it" is a cheque Move cannot currently cash.**
`notes/TODO.md` records that there is no sanctioned way to set an arbitrary width
or height — no Frame/Box primitive — and calls that rule "a wall rather than a
design" after three consumer teams each built their own Frame. Dropping every
sizing prop walks this component straight into it.

`Image` sits in the same category and already carries `width`, `height` and
`aspectRatio`. So the mistake in the prototype is not *having* sizing props; it
is inventing `normal | wide | full`, a vocabulary that exists nowhere else in the
library and describes a page width the component cannot see.

**The shape, concretely:**

```tsx
// Says nothing → sized from the artwork.
<Illustration title="How a trigger resolves" viewBox="0 0 640 360">…</Illustration>
//   inline-size: 100%; max-inline-size: 640px; aspect-ratio: 640 / 360

// Needs to say something → the words Image already uses.
<Illustration title="…" viewBox="0 0 640 360" width="24rem" />
```

Automatic when nothing is said, and when something must be said it is a prop the
reader already knows from the component next door.

### Illustration is not a general SVG wrapper

An SVG can reach a page two ways, and they are not interchangeable:

| | CSS `background-image` — **ornament** | `<img src="logo.svg">` — **Image** | inline `<svg>` — **Illustration** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Theming | via CSS, per rule |  **impossible.** A separate document: custom properties do not cross into it, `currentColor` does not resolve, no stylesheet reaches inside | tokens apply; that is the whole point |
| Caching | n/a |  cached like any asset | inlined in the DOM every render |
| Accessibility | none needed — never in the DOM | `alt` | `role="img"` + `<title>` |
| Right for | squiggles, patterns, flourishes — carries no information | logos, photos, screenshots — artwork that should NOT recolour with the theme | diagrams, empty states — drawings painted in surface/text/stroke colours |

A brand mark usually should *not* follow the theme, so `<img>` is the correct
answer for a logo and `Image` already handles it. `Illustration` exists for the
case `Image` cannot serve: a drawing that has to change colour when the theme
does. Anything that does not need theming should use `Image`, and the docs must
say so on **both** pages — `meta.ts` related entries in each direction, with the
one-line reason, not a note buried in prose on one of them.

**There is no `decorative` prop, and `title` is required** (decided with the
user, 2026-09-14). An illustration carries information by definition; a drawing
that carries none is ornament, and ornament belongs in `background-image`, where
it never enters the DOM and never needs a name. Opting out of the accessible
name would be a claim the component's own definition contradicts — so the union,
and the dev warning that would have replaced it, are both unnecessary.

The case that argued for `decorative` was the empty state, where a heading
already says "No results" and the picture repeats it. That is a content problem,
not an API one: either the title describes the PICTURE rather than restating the
message ("An empty folder with a magnifying glass"), or the picture does not earn
its place. One line in the docs, not a prop.

### Surface awareness

Decided with the user, 2026-09-14: the illustration is surface-aware, and the
caption stays in the component (`<figure>` / `<figcaption>`).

`styles/visual/surface.css` already resolves RELATIVE tokens per `[data-surface]`,
and the fills should be built on those rather than on absolute backgrounds:

| Class | Token | Resolves to |
|---|---|---|
| `illustration-ground` | `--move-surface-bg` | the ground it is actually on — page, Card, Dialog |
| `illustration-panel` | `--move-surface-alt` | a box drawn on that ground, flipped per level |
| `illustration-raised` | `--move-surface-alt-hover` | a box on a box |

**Do NOT use `--move-surface-border` for drawn lines.** It is `transparent` on a
subtle surface, which is right for a container — background contrast carries the
edge — and fatal for a diagram, whose connectors would disappear the moment the
illustration sat inside a Card. Strokes take the border ramp
(`--move-border-base` / `--move-border-emphasis`), which is visible on every
surface.

**Nesting works inside the drawing.** The surface system is an attribute plus
custom properties, so `data-surface` applies to an SVG `<g>` exactly as it does
to a div:

```svg
<g data-surface="subtle">
  <rect class="illustration-panel" />   <!-- resolves against subtle, not the page -->
</g>
```

A drawn panel flips its own subtree the way a Card does, with no React involved.

**The illustration itself should not OWN a surface.** `owns-surface` requires
painting a ground and providing `SurfaceProvider` in one act, and this
component's children are markup rather than components, so the provider would
have nothing to talk to. It stays transparent and inherits — which is also what
lets it drop into a Card, a Dialog or a bare page without being told which.

### The token surface

Designed from Move's semantic tokens, not from the prototype's classes. Two
layers, because the SVG children are written at the CALL SITE and can only be
reached by something global:

**1. Component tokens** — the definition, in the component's own scope:

```css
.root {
  /* Grounds. Surface-RELATIVE, which is the whole mechanism: these re-resolve
     under any [data-surface], so the drawing is correct on a page, inside a
     Card, inside a Dialog, without being told which. */
  --move-illustration-ground: var(--move-surface-bg);
  --move-illustration-panel: var(--move-surface-alt);
  --move-illustration-panel-raised: var(--move-surface-alt-hover);

  /* Lines. The border RAMP, deliberately not --move-surface-border, which is
     `transparent` on a subtle surface — right for a container edge, fatal for a
     connector. */
  --move-illustration-line: var(--move-border-base);
  --move-illustration-line-strong: var(--move-border-emphasis);

  /* Text */
  --move-illustration-text: var(--move-fg-base);
  --move-illustration-text-muted: var(--move-fg-muted);

  /* Accent — the one thing the drawing is pointing at */
  --move-illustration-accent: var(--move-primary);
  --move-illustration-accent-subtle: var(--move-primary-subtle);
  --move-illustration-accent-fg: var(--move-primary-fg);

  /* Status. Solid paints a mark or a line; subtle fills a region behind one. */
  --move-illustration-success: var(--move-success);
  --move-illustration-success-subtle: var(--move-success-subtle);
  --move-illustration-warning: var(--move-warning);
  --move-illustration-warning-subtle: var(--move-warning-subtle);
  --move-illustration-error: var(--move-error);
  --move-illustration-error-subtle: var(--move-error-subtle);
  --move-illustration-info: var(--move-info);
  --move-illustration-info-subtle: var(--move-info-subtle);

  /* Geometry — what makes a drawing look like it belongs to the library. */
  --move-illustration-line-width: 1.5px;
  --move-illustration-radius: var(--move-rounded-md);
  --move-illustration-dash: 4 4;
}
```

**2. Global classes** — the only vocabulary Move ships as class names rather
than tokens, because markup at the call site cannot reach a CSS module. Named so
the property is unambiguous: **a class beginning `illustration-line` strokes;
everything else fills.**

| Fills | Strokes |
|---|---|
| `illustration-ground` | `illustration-line` |
| `illustration-panel` | `illustration-line-strong` |
| `illustration-panel-raised` | `illustration-line-accent` |
| `illustration-accent` | `illustration-line-success` |
| `illustration-accent-subtle` | `illustration-line-warning` |
| `illustration-accent-fg` | `illustration-line-error` |
| `illustration-text` | `illustration-line-info` |
| `illustration-text-muted` | `illustration-line-dashed` (modifier) |
| `illustration-success` / `-warning` / `-error` / `-info` | |
| the same four `-subtle` | |

Every stroke class carries `vector-effect: non-scaling-stroke` and
`stroke-width: var(--move-illustration-line-width)`, so a hairline stays a
hairline when the drawing scales down — the thing nobody remembers by hand.
`illustration-text` also sets `font-family: var(--move-font-body)`.

**The surface mechanism, end to end.** The grounds point at `--move-surface-*`,
which `styles/visual/surface.css` redefines per `[data-surface]`. That is an
attribute plus custom properties, so it works at any depth — including inside the
drawing:

```svg
<rect class="illustration-panel" />        <!-- a box on whatever ground we are on -->
<g data-surface="subtle">
  <rect class="illustration-panel" />      <!-- a box on THAT box, flipped one level -->
  <text class="illustration-text">…</text>
</g>
```

A drawn panel flips its own subtree exactly as a Card does, and nesting composes
to any depth for free.

### Prerequisite: purity has to learn a scope

**The component is inert without this.** A wrapper's children ARE raw SVG
elements — `<path>`, `<rect>`, `<g>` — so if `check:purity` keeps flagging them
the seam is a door into a wall that is still solid.

The rule to add: raw SVG elements are legal as descendants of `<Illustration>`,
and illegal everywhere else. Purity already parses composed code with the
TypeScript compiler, so this is a matter of walking a flagged element's JSX
ancestors and allowing it when one of them is `Illustration` — scoped, not a
blanket exemption. Being inside the seam is what makes the markup legal.

A consumer's `BeatsLogo` shows the cost of not having it — one file with raw
`<svg>`/`<g>`/`<path>`/`<rect>`/`<filter>`, eight inline `style` props, a direct
animejs import and eight hardcoded `fill="white"`. They did not ignore the rule;
there was nothing to follow. Same shape as the Frame/sizing gap already in
`notes/TODO.md`: a wall rather than a design.

### Two animation gaps this surfaced

**1. Stagger order vs paint order.** Move's stagger takes its sequence from DOM
order. In SVG, DOM order IS paint order, so an artwork whose groups are ordered
by what draws on top cannot also be ordered by what animates first — and
reordering to fix the stagger changes which shapes overlap. Every stagger in the
library today is a list, where the two agree; SVG is the first place they
diverge. Either the stagger learns an explicit `data-move-stagger-order`, or
artwork like this keeps a hand-rolled delay function.

**2. No `inView` trigger.** `Root.enter` fires on mount, which is right for a
logo and wrong for an illustration below the fold. `useInView` and `Deferred`
exist in `src/hooks`, so today the answer is to gate the MOUNT rather than the
animation — which works, but means the illustration cannot simply say "reveal
when seen".

### Recommendations for Move

1. **Components to build:** one, `Illustration` — a single `<svg>` (optionally
   wrapped in `<figure>` when captioned). No sub-components; the drawing is
   children.
2. **Props consensus:** `title` (required, accessible name), `desc`, `viewBox`
   (required), `caption`, plus `width` / `height` / `aspectRatio`
   borrowed verbatim from `Image`. Dropped from the prototype: the
   `normal | wide | full` variant and `maxWidth` — see sizing above.
3. **Composition:** monolithic. React Spectrum's compound shape solves a
   different problem (an empty-state block); the caption case here is one
   optional `<figcaption>`, not a composition.
4. **Animation:** `animations?: AnimationTrigger[] | false`, defaulting to NONE.
   The prop is the library convention — every Move component merges one over its
   defaults — and a wrapper component would be a second place for animation to
   live, sitting outside the `<svg>` while the elements it staggers are inside
   it. The default is empty because a diagram that staggers itself every time it
   appears is noise; the consumer opts in, and the children opt in individually
   with `data-move-stagger`.

   Evidence this is needed: a consumer's `BeatsLogo` hand-rolls the whole thing —
   a ref, a `useEffect`, a run-once guard, a direct `animate()` import from
   animejs, a manual delay function, and `style={{opacity: 0}}` on eight groups
   to seed the start state. Every line of that is expressible as one trigger,
   except the ordering (below).
5. **Component class:** `presentational`.
6. **Default candidates (not decisions):**
   - No `decorative` prop at all; `title` required — decided with the user,
     2026-09-14. Stronger than MUI's `titleAccess`, which defaults to the
     unnamed case.
   - `preserveAspectRatio`: not exposed — medium-high. `xMidYMid meet` is right
     for every diagram; expose it only when something needs `slice`.
   - Palette classes named in full (`illustration-surface`, not `il-surface`) —
     decided with the user, 2026-09-14.
   - Token prefix `--move-illustration-*` — decided with the user, 2026-09-14.
7. **Key decisions needed before the spec:**
   - **The global class layer is public API forever.** It is the only place Move
     ships class names to consumers rather than tokens, so the vocabulary above
     should be reviewed as an API, not as styling.
   - **A check for the palette.** `check:purity` already parses composed code
     with the TypeScript compiler; it should also fail a hardcoded `fill="#…"` /
     `stroke="rgb(…)"` attribute in JSX (the classes are the only sanctioned
     route, and `check:css-hardcoded` cannot see consumer markup) and an
     `illustration-*` class that does not exist. The docs prototype already
     carries exactly that bug today — `il-pane` is used in a sample and defined
     nowhere, so the shape is silently unstyled.
   - **The docs boundary is a deliverable, not a footnote.** Both component
     pages carry the distinction above, each pointing at the other. Without it
     the two components look like duplicates and consumers will pick by name.
   - **`<text>` inside a scaled illustration.** Move can set the font family, but
     a diagram scaled to 60% has 60% labels. Either accept it, cap the downscale,
     or document that labels belong outside the SVG.
